Clinical Reference · Cardiology

STEMI — ST-Elevation MI

On this page
STEMI = acute total (or near-total) coronary occlusion causing transmural ischemia — ST-elevation on ECG + a rising troponin — where time is muscle and emergent reperfusion (primary PCI or, if unavailable in time, fibrinolysis) is the single highest-yield intervention.
Type 1 MI · plaque rupture + thrombus FMC-to-device ≤90 min (PCI-capable) Door-to-needle ≤30 min (lytic) In-hospital mortality ~5–6%; ~50% if cardiogenic shock Anchor: dual antiplatelet + anticoagulant + emergent reperfusion
Shared

Pathophysiology & diagnosis

🧬

Mechanism — the story of a dying wall

An atherosclerotic plaque is not a smooth narrowing — it is a lipid core wrapped in a thin fibrous cap under a layer of inflamed endothelium. When that cap ruptures or erodes, the highly thrombogenic core (tissue factor, collagen) is exposed to flowing blood. Platelets instantly adhere and activate, amplifying through three parallel loops — thromboxane A₂ (COX-1), ADP (P2Y12), and final-common-pathway GP IIb/IIIa cross-linking — while tissue factor fires the coagulation cascade to generate thrombin and a fibrin mesh. In STEMI, the result is a fully occlusive, fibrin-rich thrombus: flow stops, and the entire thickness of the wall downstream loses its oxygen supply (transmural ischemia → ST elevation).

Necrosis then advances as a wavefront — from subendocardium outward to epicardium over roughly 1–6 hours. Myocardium is not dead the instant the artery closes; there is a shrinking window of salvageable muscle at risk. That is why every guideline is obsessed with minutes: reopening the artery early rescues the outer wall, preserves ejection fraction, and prevents the downstream cascade of pump failure, malignant arrhythmia, and mechanical rupture.

Think of the coronary artery as a garden hose feeding one section of lawn. A ruptured plaque is a wad of gum jammed in the hose — water stops completely, and the grass browns from the tips inward. Aspirin and P2Y12 blockers stop new gum from sticking; heparin stops the water itself from clotting around it; the balloon (PCI) or the clot-buster (lytic) physically clears the plug. The longer the water is off, the more lawn you lose — and dead lawn doesn't grow back.
Plaque rupture → platelet + coagulation amplification → occlusive thrombus → transmural ischemia → wavefront of necrosis. Each drug class is annotated at the step it interrupts.
Coronary anatomy: LAD (anterior wall/septum, V1–V4), LCx (lateral, I/aVL/V5–6), RCA (inferior II/III/aVF + RV).
Chris Talbot, Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0
Ruptured atheroma with exposed lipid core — the trigger event for Type 1 MI.
Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0
The whole drug list maps onto this one cascade. Aspirin blocks COX-1/TXA₂; ticagrelor/prasugrel/clopidogrel block the P2Y12 ADP receptor; GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors block the final platelet cross-link; heparin/bivalirudin block thrombin; fibrinolytics (tenecteplase) convert plasminogen → plasmin to dissolve the fibrin mesh; β-blockers cut myocardial O₂ demand and arrhythmia; statins stabilize the plaque; ACEi/ARB + MRA block the maladaptive remodeling that follows the infarct.
⏱️

The reperfusion decision — time is muscle

Everything in STEMI care flows from one branch point: can this patient get primary PCI fast enough? If yes, PCI wins on every endpoint. If a PCI-capable cath lab cannot deliver a device within 120 minutes of first medical contact (FMC), give a fibrinolytic within 30 minutes of arrival and transfer for angiography (pharmacoinvasive strategy).

Reperfusion algorithm with the guideline time targets (2025 ACC/AHA ACS). Fibrinolysis is a bridge — every lysed patient still goes to angiography.
"Time is muscle" is literal: roughly 1–2 million myocytes die per minute of untreated occlusion. Mortality benefit of reperfusion is greatest in the first 2–3 hours and decays thereafter — but reperfusion still helps out to 12 h (and beyond if ongoing ischemia/instability).

Biomarker & imaging interpretation

🧫

Why each abnormal lab moves — and what fools it

Cardinal rule: STEMI is an ECG + clinical diagnosis — do not wait for a biomarker to reperfuse. Troponin can be normal in the first 1–3 hours because release lags necrosis. Biomarkers are for confirmation, infarct sizing, and catching reinfarction.

LabDirection & timingMechanismConfounders / false movers
High-sensitivity troponin I/TRises 1–3 h, peaks 12–24 h, stays up 7–14 dReleased from necrotic myocyte cytosol then structural pool; exquisitely cardiac-specificRaised falsely-attributed: CKD (reduced clearance), sepsis, PE, myocarditis, HF, tachyarrhythmia, Takotsubo. These are Type 2 injury — not an indication to lyse
CK-MBRises 3–6 h, peaks ~24 h, normalizes 48–72 hMyocardial isoenzyme of creatine kinaseSkeletal muscle injury, rhabdo, heavy exercise; useful for reinfarction because it clears fast (a re-rise flags a new event)
Potassium / magnesiumTrend; replete aggressivelyLow K⁺/Mg²⁺ lower the VF threshold post-infarctKeep K⁺ >4.0, Mg²⁺ >2.0; hemolyzed sample falsely raises K⁺
CreatinineMay rise post-cathContrast-induced nephropathy; low output in shockGuides anticoagulant renal dosing; pre-hydrate
LactateRises in shockAnaerobic metabolism from hypoperfusionMarker of shock severity + clearance target; also raised by epinephrine, metformin, liver failure
BNP / NT-proBNPRises with wall stressVentricular stretch from LV dysfunctionAge, CKD, AF raise it; obesity lowers it — supports HF, not diagnostic of MI

Key imaging findings — when they appear

StudyWhen to orderFinding & meaning
12-lead ± right-sided/posterior ECGWithin 10 min; V4R for every inferior MI; V7–V9 if posterior suspectedST-elevation localizes the culprit; reciprocal depression supports it; V4R elevation = RV infarct
Coronary angiographyEmergent (primary PCI) or 2–24 h post-lysisCulprit occlusion (TIMI 0–1); goal of PCI is TIMI 3 flow
Transthoracic echo (TTE)Inpatient; urgent if new murmur/collapseRegional wall-motion abnormality, LVEF, LV thrombus, and mechanical complications (MR, VSD, effusion/tamponade)
Chest X-rayOn arrival if HF suspected; before/with reperfusionPulmonary edema (Killip), cardiomegaly; screens for aortic contour (dissection mimic)
Cardiac MRISubacute, selectedInfarct size/viability, microvascular obstruction; distinguishes myocarditis/Takotsubo when angiogram is clean

Presentation — recognize & refer

🔍

Symptoms & signs — frequency + why it happens

An active STEMI is not a clinic diagnosis — the clinic job is to recognize it and activate EMS, and to run tight secondary prevention for everyone post-MI. Frequencies below are for acute MI presentation.

Symptom / sign~FreqWhy it happens
Chest pain/pressure (retrosternal, >20 min)~80%Ischemic myocardium releases adenosine/lactate/bradykinin activating cardiac C-fibers; referred via T1–T4 dermatomes
Diaphoresis~50%Sympathetic surge from pain + falling stroke volume → catecholamine-driven sweating
Dyspnea~40–50%Acute LV dysfunction ↑ LV end-diastolic pressure → pulmonary congestion
Radiation to arm/jaw/shoulder~40%Convergence of cardiac + somatic afferents in the dorsal horn (referred pain)
Nausea / vomiting~30%Vagal activation, esp. inferior MI (Bezold–Jarisch reflex)
Anginal equivalents (fatigue, epigastric) — women, elderly, DM~30%Autonomic neuropathy + atypical afferent processing blunt classic pain
Syncope / presyncope~10%Arrhythmia (VT/brady) or acute pump failure dropping cerebral perfusion
Sudden cardiac death as first presentation~5–10%Ischemia-triggered VF, often within the first hour
Any active ischemic chest pain in clinic → immediate 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes; if STE present, call 911 / activate STEMI system now — do not drive the patient yourself, do not wait for troponin.

Post-MI GDMT — first-line → escalation

💊

The secondary-prevention stack (ACC/AHA 2025 ACS)

1
Antiplatelet foundation — DAPT
Aspirin lifelong + a P2Y12 inhibitor ≥12 months
▾
Aspirin blocks COX-1/TXA₂; the P2Y12 inhibitor blocks the ADP amplification loop. Together they suppress the two dominant platelet activation pathways that drive stent thrombosis and recurrent atherothrombosis.
DrugStart / LoadTitrationTarget / maintWhy / when defaultIf intolerant / alt
Aspirin162–325 mg chewed (acute)—81 mg daily, indefiniteCOX-1/TXA₂ blockade; lifelong backboneTrue allergy → aspirin desensitization (preferred); else clopidogrel monotherapy
Ticagrelor180 mg load—90 mg BID ×12 mo (then 60 mg BID if extended)Reversible P2Y12; co-preferred (PLATO). Keep ASA ≤100 mgDyspnea/intolerance → clopidogrel
Prasugrel60 mg load (at PCI)5 mg if <60 kg or ≥75 y10 mg dailyIrreversible P2Y12; co-preferred (TRITON, ISAR-REACT 5)Contraindicated w/ prior stroke/TIA → ticagrelor or clopidogrel
Clopidogrel600 mg load (PCI)—75 mg dailyDefault when ticagrelor/prasugrel not tolerated, on OAC, or high bleeding riskCYP2C19 loss-of-function → poor response
De-escalation: after 1–3 months of DAPT in patients who tolerated it, transition to P2Y12 (ticagrelor) monotherapy to cut bleeding while preserving ischemic protection (2025 ACS).
2
High-intensity statin ± ezetimibe ± PCSK9
"Lower is better" — LDL goal <55 mg/dL
▾
Statins do far more than lower LDL — they stabilize the fibrous cap, restore endothelial function, and blunt inflammation, directly attacking the rupture-prone lesion that caused the MI.
DrugStartTitrationTarget / maxWhy it worksIf intolerant / alt
Atorvastatin80 mg daily (start in-hospital)—80 mg (max)HMG-CoA reductase inhibition + plaque stabilization; ≥50% LDL dropMyalgia → rosuvastatin or ↓ dose/alternate-day

On max statin + ezetimibe, if LDL ≥55–70 mg/dL → add a PCSK9 inhibitor. Recheck lipids 4–12 wk after each change.

Especially EF ≤40%, anterior MI, HTN, DM

β-blockers cut O₂ demand and arrhythmia; ACEi/ARB block angiotensin II to prevent the adverse LV remodeling (dilation/thinning) that follows a transmural infarct.

Comorbidity interactions

🔗

How comorbidities change STEMI course & therapy

ComorbidityEffect on courseEffect on management
CKD↑ mortality, contrast nephropathy risk, ↑ bleedingMinimize contrast + pre-hydrate; enoxaparin 1 mg/kg daily if CrCl <30; avoid fondaparinux/eplerenone in advanced CKD; radial access
DiabetesHigher event rates, atypical presentationAggressive GDMT; add SGLT2i/GLP-1 RA; avoid glucose extremes inpatient
Atrial fibrillation on OACNeeds anticoagulation + antiplatelets → bleedingDrop aspirin early; DOAC + clopidogrel (AUGUSTUS). Brief triple therapy only periprocedurally
Prior bleeding / anemiaHigh bleeding risk on DAPTRadial access, shorter DAPT, P2Y12 monotherapy, bivalirudin, PPI
Cocaine-associated MICoronary vasospasm + thrombosisAVOID β-blockers (unopposed α); use benzodiazepines, nitrates, CCB, phentolamine
Advanced age (≥75)↑ ICH + bleedingHalf-dose TNK if lysed; avoid prasugrel; careful anticoagulant dosing
Drugs to avoid / use with caution in STEMI: NSAIDs other than aspirin (↑ reinfarction, rupture, death — stop them); prasugrel with prior stroke/TIA (harm) and generally in ≥75 y or <60 kg; β-blockers in acute cocaine, decompensated HF/shock, RV infarct, or high-grade AV block; nitrates in RV infarct or recent PDE-5 inhibitor; short-acting nifedipine.

Monitor

Titration & follow-up cadence

📈

What to recheck, and when

  • Lipids: 4–12 weeks after starting/changing a statin, then annually. Target LDL <55 mg/dL and ≥50% reduction.
  • Electrolytes/renal: within 1–2 weeks of ACEi/ARB/MRA start and after each dose change (watch K⁺, creatinine).
  • Echo: reassess LVEF ~40 days post-MI — if EF ≤35% on optimal GDMT, refer for primary-prevention ICD.
  • Visits: early post-discharge visit within 1–2 weeks; confirm DAPT adherence, cardiac-rehab enrollment, smoking cessation.
  • HbA1c/BP: per comorbidity; keep BP <130/80.
Escalate

When to refer / admit

🚑

Red flags → ED / STEMI activation

Active ischemic chest pain with ST-elevation on ECG → activate 911/STEMI system immediately. Give aspirin 162–325 mg chewed while awaiting EMS.
Post-MI patients: recurrent/rest angina, new dyspnea/orthopnea, syncope, palpitations with presyncope, abrupt severe chest pain (possible stent thrombosis), or significant bleeding on DAPT — send to ED, don't manage in clinic.
🛏️ Wards — reperfusion, post-PCI care & complications
Admit

Reperfusion first, then admit

📋

Every STEMI is admitted — the question is the reperfusion route

All STEMIs are admitted to a monitored bed (telemetry step-down or CCU/ICU depending on stability). The floor/step-down manages uncomplicated post-primary-PCI patients; shock, refractory arrhythmia, or mechanical complications belong in the ICU.

Reperfusion route: PCI-capable center → primary PCI, FMC-to-device ≤90 min. Non-PCI center → transfer if PCI achievable ≤120 min of FMC (door-in-door-out ≤30 min); otherwise fibrinolysis, door-to-needle ≤30 min, then transfer for angiography 2–24 h (pharmacoinvasive).
Fibrinolysis — absolute contraindicationsRelative contraindications
Any prior intracranial hemorrhage (ever)SBP >180 / DBP >110 on presentation or chronic severe HTN
Known structural cerebral vascular lesion (AVM)Ischemic stroke >3 months ago; dementia
Malignant intracranial neoplasmTraumatic/prolonged (>10 min) CPR; major surgery <3 wk
Ischemic stroke within 3 months (except acute <4.5 h)Recent (2–4 wk) internal bleeding; noncompressible punctures
Suspected aortic dissectionPregnancy; active peptic ulcer
Active bleeding / bleeding diathesisCurrent oral anticoagulant use
Significant closed-head/facial trauma <3 months—

Source: 2013 ACCF/AHA STEMI guideline.

Monitor

What to trend + complications

📈

Daily assessment & in-hospital complications

  • Rhythm: telemetry for VT/VF (first 24–48 h), AF, AV block. Accelerated idioventricular rhythm is usually a benign reperfusion marker.
  • Hemodynamics/volume: BP, HR, JVP, lungs, urine output — watch for evolving HF.
  • Labs: Hgb (bleeding), K⁺/Mg²⁺ (keep >4.0 / >2.0), renal function (contrast).
  • Access site: hematoma, bruit (pseudoaneurysm), distal pulses.
ComplicationClueAction
Recurrent ischemia / stent thrombosisRecurrent pain + new ST changesEmergent re-cath
VT/VFHighest risk first 24–48 hDefibrillate/ACLS; correct K⁺/Mg²⁺; β-blocker; reperfuse
AV block / bradycardiaEsp. inferior MIAtropine → transcutaneous/transvenous pacing
Heart failure / pulmonary edemaRising O₂ need, ralesDiurese, afterload reduction; escalate if refractory
PericarditisPleuritic pain; early or Dressler (weeks)Aspirin/colchicine; avoid NSAIDs/steroids acutely
Escalate

When to call ICU

⬆️

Floor → ICU triggers

Transfer to ICU for any of: SBP <90 / cardiogenic shock or need for pressor/inotrope; sustained VT/VF or electrical storm; high-grade AV block requiring pacing; acute pulmonary edema / respiratory failure needing NIV or intubation; mechanical complication (new murmur, tamponade); or recurrent ischemia requiring emergent re-intervention.
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness + where they go

Discharge readiness: hemodynamically stable ≥24 h, no ongoing ischemia or unstable arrhythmia, ambulating safely, GDMT started and tolerated, education (meds, DAPT adherence, warning signs) done, follow-up + cardiac rehab arranged. Uncomplicated primary-PCI STEMI can be discharged as early as 48–72 h.

Home + cardiac rehab

Most patients: stable, independent, GDMT tolerated. Rehab referral is Class 1.

Home health

Home + skilled nursing/therapy visits for wound/med management.

SNF

Deconditioned/elderly needing 24h skilled nursing, <3h therapy/day.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Can tolerate ≥3h therapy/day, ≥2 disciplines (e.g., post-arrest deconditioning).

LTAC

Prolonged complex care (e.g., vent weaning after shock) >25 days.

Hospice / palliative

Massive infarct with refractory shock + goals favoring comfort.
🫀 ICU — cardiogenic shock, mechanical complications & arrhythmia
Admit

ICU triggers & SCAI shock stages

🚨

When STEMI belongs in the unit

Cardiogenic shock complicates ~5–10% of STEMI and is the leading cause of in-hospital STEMI death. Emergent revascularization of the culprit is the single most important intervention (SHOCK trial).

SCAI stageStateBedside~In-hospital mortality
A — At riskLarge MI, no shockNormal exam~0.6%
B — BeginningCompensated↓BP or tachycardia, no hypoperfusion~2.7%
C — ClassicHypoperfusion needs supportCold/clammy, oliguria, lactate ↑; needs pressor/inotrope/MCS~21.5%
D — DeterioratingFailing to respondNeeds escalation of support~54.3%
E — ExtremisCirculatory collapseRefractory, often CPR/ECMO~90.6%
RV infarction (accompanies ~30–50% of inferior STEMI): triad of hypotension + clear lungs + elevated JVP; confirm ST-elevation in V4R. Treat with fluids, avoid nitrates/diuretics/morphine, maintain AV synchrony, add dobutamine if fluids insufficient.
Monitor

Monitoring & access

🩸

Lines, labs, targets

  • Arterial line for continuous BP; target MAP ≥65.
  • Central access for vasopressors; consider PA (Swan-Ganz) catheter to guide shock therapy (differentiate RV vs LV failure, measure CI, PCWP, SVR, mixed venous sat).
  • Trend: lactate/lactate clearance, urine output, mixed venous O₂ sat, serial echo.
  • STAT echo for any new murmur, sudden collapse, or recurrent shock → rule out mechanical complication.
Mechanical complication (days 3–5, up to 2 wk)ClueAction
Papillary muscle rupture → acute MRFlash pulmonary edema, new MR murmur (posteromedial, single RCA supply)Afterload reduction/MCS bridge → emergent surgery
Ventricular septal defectNew harsh holosystolic murmur, O₂ step-up RA→RV, biventricular failureMCS bridge → surgical/percutaneous closure
Free wall ruptureTamponade, PEA, sudden deathEmergent pericardiocentesis + surgery
LV aneurysm / pseudoaneurysmPersistent ST-elevation weeks laterPseudoaneurysm (contained rupture) → surgery

Which drip, why, and the dose

AgentReceptors / mechanismDose rangeHemodynamic effectWhen to pick
Norepinephrineα1 ≫ β10.05–0.5 mcg/kg/min (up to ~1)↑SVR, mild ↑COFirst-line in cardiogenic shock (SOAP II: less arrhythmia/death vs dopamine)
Dobutamineβ1 > β2 (inodilator)2.5–20 mcg/kg/min↑CO, ↓SVRFirst-line inotrope for low output; may drop BP
DopamineDose-dependent: DA → β1 → α12–20 mcg/kg/min↑CO, ↑HR, ↑SVR (high)Largely superseded (more tachyarrhythmia)
Epinephrineβ1/β2 (low) → α1 (high)0.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min↑CO, ↑SVRRefractory shock; ↑lactate/arrhythmia
VasopressinV1 (non-adrenergic)0.03–0.04 units/min (fixed)↑SVRCatecholamine-sparing adjunct
MilrinonePDE-3 inhibitor (inodilator)0.125–0.75 mcg/kg/min↑CO, ↓SVR/PVRRV failure/pulmonary HTN; renally cleared, causes hypotension
In cardiogenic shock the primary problem is a failing pump, not vasodilation — so you pair a pressor (norepinephrine) to keep coronary perfusion pressure up with an inotrope (dobutamine/milrinone) to raise cardiac output. Every catecholamine costs myocardial O₂ and arrhythmia risk, so use the lowest effective dose and move early to mechanical support.
Airway

Respiratory support & vent

🌬️

NIV vs intubate; initial settings

Give oxygen only if SpO₂ <90% (AVOID-O2 — routine O₂ in normoxia offers no benefit and may harm). NIV (CPAP/BiPAP) for cardiogenic pulmonary edema reduces work of breathing and preload; intubate for depressed consciousness (post-arrest), refractory hypoxemia, or exhaustion.

Positive-pressure ventilation reduces LV afterload (helps pulmonary edema) but reduces preload — use caution in RV infarction or hypovolemia, where it can precipitate hypotension.
Rescue

Mechanical circulatory support & rescue

⚙️

Devices, arrhythmia & post-arrest care

DeviceEvidenceRole now
IABP (intra-aortic balloon pump)IABP-SHOCK II (2012): negative — no 30-day mortality benefitNo longer routine in AMI shock
Microaxial flow pump (Impella CP)DanGer Shock (2024): 180-d mortality 45.8% vs 58.5% (NNT ~8), more bleeding/limb ischemia/RRTClass 2a in selected STEMI cardiogenic shock

IABP counterpulsation — historically first-line, now non-routine after IABP-SHOCK II.
Wikimedia Commons · CC
Emergent culprit revascularization is the single most important shock intervention.
Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA
In shock, treat the culprit only (CULPRIT-SHOCK) — routine acute multivessel PCI worsens outcomes; complete revascularization is for the stable STEMI patient.

Arrhythmia & post-arrest

  • VT/VF: defibrillation/ACLS; amiodarone or lidocaine for recurrent VT; β-blocker + correct ischemia/electrolytes for electrical storm; urgent revascularization.
  • Complete heart block: atropine → transcutaneous → transvenous pacing. Inferior-MI block is usually transient (AV-nodal, atropine-responsive); anterior-MI block is infranodal and signals extensive infarct.
  • Post-cardiac-arrest: targeted temperature management 32–36 °C and avoid fever; emergent angiography if STEMI on ECG; delay neuroprognostication ≥72 h.
Downgrade

When to downgrade

⬇️

De-escalation to step-down/floor

Downgrade when: off vasopressors/inotropes ≥12–24 h with MAP ≥65 and clearing lactate; no sustained/malignant arrhythmia ≥24 h; extubated with stable respiratory status; mechanical complications addressed; adequate urine output. Not yet if: still requiring any pressor/inotrope, unstable rhythm, active ischemia, or MCS device in place.

ICU disposition after complex courses may route through step-down → floor → cardiac rehab, or to LTAC (prolonged vent weaning) or palliative care for refractory shock with goals favoring comfort.
